We're working on both the spec and the code, as a chain. This first step changes the spec only, located in ./spec; the code is changed in the next step.

Write the spec so it describes the application as it should be once the prompt is met, and constrains the code. Once you finish, the spec will be built and the same prompt sent to a coding agent, with your reply, to change the code to match it; so end your reply by saying what you changed in the spec and which anchors the code should follow.

When the work is about Suspense, its modes, its prompts, or its questions, or you are to write a prompt or a question for the user, first read .suspense/suspense-fluency.md once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Suspense works.

Before creating or editing any .pi file, read .suspense/fluency.md once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Piton is written.

Open a .pi file only to change it. Once you have changed the spec, run `piton check` and fix every error it reports, then run `piton build` and check the result in the refreshed reference under .claude/reference, not by reading the source again. Never finish with a spec that `piton check` or `piton build` reports errors in.

Once you have read what the change depends on, and before your first change, write the constraints this task must meet to .suspense/history/1791820865-FixAwkwardAlignmentIssues.understanding.md, once. Rewrite it only when a constraint in it turns out to be wrong, never after each page you read. It is a Markdown list and nothing else: one line per constraint, at most twelve, each a single short, specific statement of what must be true, written as a link to the compiled reference file it comes from, such as `- [The chain tab has no bottom border in combined mode](.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chain)`. Only list what the spec says; leave out anything you are deciding yourself. Replace a constraint when you learn it was wrong rather than adding another.

End with a reply of a few sentences saying what changed, or for a question, the answer, not a recap of the work or of what you read.

## Sent Prompt

### Description

A task's header is one slim line, 32 pixels tall, across the view's full width, and nothing more: it never shows the prompt, the compiled markdown, or the hidden anchor's name. From left to right, 8 pixels in, come a bar 4 pixels wide with corners rounded 2 pixels, inset 6 pixels from the header's top and bottom, in the colour of the mode the task was sent in, as the [PromptModes](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes) colours it, the step's mode for a step of a chain, telling where it came from; its status, a spinner while it is under way and its status label, with its elapsed time beside it, as the status says; then its summary, in small text, cut off with an ellipsis; then, at its right, its buttons. The header is on the tab bar's background, faintly tinted the mode's colour, a sixth of its strength, never the stronger tint it had.

### Summary

The summary is a short line saying what the task is for: its title, the words its hidden anchor was named from, as "Chat titles from the agent", or, where it was named at random or not yet named, the first line of its prompt as typed. For a step of a chain, the step's label, "Spec", "Code", or "Spec follow-up", comes first, in its mode's colour, then the chain's summary. Hovering the summary shows the prompt's first lines as its tooltip.

### Buttons

At the header's right, small ghost buttons, 24 pixels tall, 4 pixels apart. "Pause", with a pause icon, while the task is running, pauses it, and "Resume", with a play icon, in its place while it is paused, resumes it, as the [PromptSending](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending) says. "Stop", with a stop icon, while the task is building, compiling, running, or paused, cancels it as Cancel does, as the [PromptSending](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending) says, and is gone once it is over. "View all", with a list icon, opens the task in the right sidebar's Tasks tab, as the [TasksTab](../../../ui/components/right-sidebar/tasks/index.md#tasks-tab) opens a task, where its prompt, steps, details, parameters, and the rest of its actions are, opening the sidebar first if it is closed. The header has no Resend, no Send to Spec or Send to Code, and no other button: those are in the Tasks tab.

## Status

### Description

A task's status is a coloured label that spells it out: "Building" in blue, "Compiling" in cyan, "Running" in yellow, "Done" in green, "Failed" in red, "Cancelled" in orange, "Paused" in the theme's warning colour for a task paused to be resumed, as the PromptSending says, "Stopped" in grey for a chain that stopped short of a step it was to run, and "Not recorded" in grey for a task from the history with no record of its run. The labels are readable in both light and dark mode.

### Elapsed

Beside its status label, a task shows how long it has been under way, from when it was sent, building and compiling included, in small muted tabular figures: minutes and seconds, "0:42" or "12:05", with hours ahead of them once it reaches an hour, "1:02:33". While the task is building, compiling, or running, it counts up every second, so a task that seems stuck can be told from one that has only just started. Once the task is over, however it ended, it stops and stays at how long the task took. It shows wherever the status label does, the latest task's header and the heading of each previous task, including a task running in the other lane. A task from the history whose record holds no start and end, as one recorded before they were kept, shows how long it took as well as can be told, from the second its history file is named by to when its record was written, with "≈" before it, as "≈ 4:12", its tooltip saying it is approximate; one where neither can be told shows none.
In the Tasks tab, every task's row shows how long it took, as the latest task's header does, though not beside its status: done, failed, or cancelled alike, and a task still running there counting up. A chain's parent row shows the time its steps took together, from when its first step was sent to when its last ended, and each step's heading beneath it its own. The times line up, right-aligned in their own column of the heading, just before its buttons, so the list reads as a column of durations that can be compared at a glance, and a long one stands out.

### Output Rate

While a run is writing a reply, its status shows how fast the harness is writing beside its elapsed time, muted, in the same small tabular figures, such as "42 tok/s": the reply's output tokens as they stream in, counted from the harness's own usage as it reports it, or, where it reports none mid-turn, estimated from the text streamed at about four characters a token, over the time the current reply has taken so far, from its first streamed text, smoothed over the last few seconds so it doesn't flicker. It shows only while the harness is writing: while it waits on a tool call, runs a command, or hasn't yet begun to reply, the rate is left out, never shown as zero.
Once a run is over, its task header, and a question's answer, show its average output rate in the same place, muted: the output tokens the harness reported for the run divided by the time it spent waiting on the model, as Claude Code reports it in its result's API duration, or, for a harness that reports no such time, the time the application measured from each turn's start to the usage reported at its end, leaving out the time spent in tool calls. Its tooltip says how it was worked out, "Output tokens over time waiting on the model" or "Output tokens over time writing, as measured". A rate the harness gives too little to work out, as a run that reported no output tokens, or took no measurable time, is left out rather than shown as zero.
The rate shows for every run that writes a reply, whatever it was sent in, Code, Chain steps, Spec, Freeform, and questions alike, whatever their sandbox. In a task's slim header it sits right after the elapsed time, muted, before the summary, and in the Tasks tab beside the time of a running row. It is worked out from the streamed reply's own deltas as they arrive, and from the usage each message reports, never only from the run's final result, so it shows as soon as the reply begins and isn't waiting for the run to end; the average once it ends is from the result's own figures, Claude Code's `duration_api_ms` among them.

## Rows

Every task is one row, 28 pixels tall, as a queued prompt's is, and every row in every section is laid out in the same columns, so their parts line up down the whole list: a bar in its mode's colour, as the [PromptModes](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/modes/index.md#prompt-modes) colours it, 4 pixels wide with corners rounded 2 pixels, inset from the row's edges, 4 pixels from its left and 6 from its top and bottom, so it stands as a short rounded pill rather than running edge to edge, and the bars of rows one above another never touch; then a lead column 20 pixels wide, holding a Previous row's checkbox, a Queued row's drag grip, and nothing in a Running row, the column kept empty rather than closed up where there is nothing in it; then a status column 20 pixels wide, a spinner while it is under way, a tick, cross, or dash once it has ended, or, queued, its place in the queue; then the first line of its prompt, cut off with an ellipsis; then, at its right, muted, how long it took, or has been running, as the [MessageList](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/message-list/index.md#message-list) writes it, right-aligned in a column of its own, and any buttons the row has after it. So a row's status and its text start at the same place whether it has a checkbox, a grip, or neither, and so do the section headings' titles, set in from their chevrons to line up with the rows' text.
A chain, or any task of more than one step, is one row like any other, its status the chain's as a whole, with its step count muted beside its time. In Previous and Queued its steps are never listed in the list; they are shown once it is opened, as its chain steps say. While it is Running, it is expanded in the Running group: its row, then a row for each of its steps beneath it, in the order they run, sent or still to send, each a 28 pixel row in the same columns, its text set in 16 pixels further and labelled "Spec", "Code", or "Spec follow-up" in that step's mode colour, with the step's own status, a tick, cross, or dash for one that has ended, a spinner for the one running, "Queued" with its place in its lane's queue for one waiting there, and a muted "Next" for one that will be sent once the step before it finishes, and "Waiting" for any after that, every step listed from the moment the chain is sent, as its chain steps say, each with its own time. A step being queued shows here, as part of its chain, rather than among the queued prompts, though it keeps its place in its lane's queue. The steps can't be collapsed, and once the chain is over they go with it into Previous as a single row. Clicking the chain's row, or any of its steps, opens the chain, its Steps section showing the same.
A chain's rows are joined by its colour: in place of each row's own bar, one bar in the Chain colour, purple, 4 pixels wide with corners rounded 2 pixels, runs unbroken down the left of the chain's row and every step row beneath it, Spec, Code, Spec follow-up, and any step added, from 6 pixels below the top of the chain's row to 6 pixels above the bottom of its last step's, across the gaps between the rows, so the chain reads as one block. The steps' own modes show in their labels' colours, never in a bar of their own. It is drawn the same in a chain's Steps section once opened, and grows or shrinks with the chain as a step is added. A single task, not part of a chain, keeps its own bar. Clicking a row opens it, as below, and the row stays highlighted while it is open. A row in Previous opens in the tab like any other, done, failed, cancelled, or not recorded alike, and its output opens in a body tab of its own at the same time, so every previous task can be read whole, its header, output table, and changed files, however old, as long as its record is in the history. One whose record can't be read opens all the same, saying why, muted, in place of its output. Hovering a row shows its prompt's first lines in its tooltip.

use /lib

export anchor MessageListStatus:
    description:
        A task's status is a coloured label that spells it out: "Building" in
        blue, "Compiling" in cyan, "Running" in yellow, "Done" in green,
        "Failed" in red, "Cancelled" in orange, "Paused" in the theme's warning colour for a task paused to be resumed, as the PromptSending says, "Stopped" in grey for a chain that stopped short of a step it was to run, and "Not recorded" in grey for
        a task from the history with no record of its run. The labels are
        readable in both light and dark mode.

    elapsed:
        Beside its status label, a task shows how long it has been under way,
        from when it was sent, building and compiling included, in small
        muted tabular figures: minutes and seconds, "0:42" or "12:05", with
        hours ahead of them once it reaches an hour, "1:02:33". While the task
        is building, compiling, or running, it counts up every second, so a
        task that seems stuck can be told from one that has only just
        started. Once the task is over, however it ended, it stops and stays
        at how long the task took. It shows wherever the status label does,
        the latest task's header and the heading of each previous task,
        including a task running in the other lane. A task from the history
        whose record holds no start and end, as one recorded before they
        were kept, shows how long it took as well as can be told, from the
        second its history file is named by to when its record was written,
        with "≈" before it, as "≈ 4:12", its tooltip saying it is
        approximate; one where neither can be told shows none.

        In the Tasks tab, every task's row shows how long it
        took, as the latest task's header does, though not beside its status: done,
        failed, or cancelled alike, and a task still running there counting
        up. A chain's parent row shows the time its steps took together,
        from when its first step was sent to when its last ended, and each
        step's heading beneath it its own. The times line up, right-aligned
        in their own column of the heading, just before its buttons, so the
        list reads as a column of durations that can be compared at a
        glance, and a long one stands out.

    outputRate:
        While a run is writing a reply, its status shows how fast the harness
        is writing beside its elapsed time, muted, in the same small tabular
        figures, such as "42 tok/s": the reply's output tokens as they stream
        in, counted from the harness's own usage as it reports it, or, where
        it reports none mid-turn, estimated from the text streamed at about
        four characters a token, over the time the current reply has taken so
        far, from its first streamed text, smoothed over the last few seconds
        so it doesn't flicker. It shows only while the harness is writing:
        while it waits on a tool call, runs a command, or hasn't yet begun to
        reply, the rate is left out, never shown as zero.

        Once a run is over, its task header, and a question's answer, show
        its average output rate in the same place, muted: the output tokens
        the harness reported for the run divided by the time it spent waiting
        on the model, as Claude Code reports it in its result's API duration,
        or, for a harness that reports no such time, the time the application
        measured from each turn's start to the usage reported at its end,
        leaving out the time spent in tool calls. Its tooltip says how it was
        worked out, "Output tokens over time waiting on the model" or
        "Output tokens over time writing, as measured". A rate the harness
        gives too little to work out, as a run that reported no output
        tokens, or took no measurable time, is left out rather than shown as
        zero.

        The rate shows for every run that writes a reply, whatever it was
        sent in, Code, Chain steps, Spec, Freeform, and questions alike,
        whatever their sandbox. In a task's slim header it sits right
        after the elapsed time, muted, before the summary, and in the Tasks
        tab beside the time of a running row. It is worked out from the
        streamed reply's own deltas as they arrive, and from the usage each
        message reports, never only from the run's final result, so it shows
        as soon as the reply begins and isn't waiting for the run to end; the
        average once it ends is from the result's own figures, Claude Code's
        `duration_api_ms` among them.

I added an Alignment rule for the task status line, so the spinner, the "Running" label and the time sit on one evenly spaced line. `piton check` and `piton build` both pass.

I assumed the screenshot is the task header's status line and the icon at its left is the progress spinner; if that icon is something else, tell me and I'll cover it too.

**What changed in the spec:** a new "Alignment" section under the message list's Status, in `spec/scope/prompt-mode/message-list/Status.pi`:
- **One line:** the spinner, the label, the elapsed time and the output rate are all centred vertically, so none sits higher or lower than the others. The label's text and the times share one baseline and one small text size.
- **Spinner:** 12 pixels square, in the status label's colour, and never taller than the label's text.
- **Label:** a pill 20 pixels tall, with 6 pixels on each side of its text, a 1 pixel border and faint fill in its own colour, and corners rounded 4 pixels. The 20 pixel height and 4 pixel corners are my own choices, since the spec gave no size for the pill.
- **Spacing:** the same 6 pixel gap between spinner and label, label and time, and time and rate.

The code should follow `.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/message-list/index.md#alignment`, alongside the existing `#status`, `#elapsed` and `#output-rate`.
